text: Human dignity is not a constraint on a technical system — it is the first-order technical requirement.
The infinity symbol is not decorative. It signals that the covenant the owner makes with this work does not expire.
This is a system that breathes.

She slid from the womb onto soil — no cloth, no hand. The cord hung, purple, chewed by stone. She shivered, and the goosebumps rose like thorns. The others thought: Weak. She clawed at the air. Fists closed on nothing. Where her nails caught grass, she twisted. A loop. A knot. A beginning.
If the point is greedy, the river will punish it.
We made a suggestion the river agreed with.
If it keeps working, it's a law. If not, it was a good day.
Write what happened, not what should have. One mark per work. No fat. Memory goes in backs and feet.
Teach it to breathe. Good.
Don't smile at it. It will remember your teeth and crack there.
Now it remembers you. — Ya-la, pressing her thumbprint into the repaired oven wall.
Home lives in the small change.
Don't be brave. Be awake.
A thing that learns is worth more than a thing that is made.
The gap that moves is the gap that lives.
Some things are only borrowed. When they go home, let them.
A thing can be useful and beautiful. They are not enemies.
Fire is a gift, but it is also a teacher. It reminds us that we can begin again.
The path that disappears is not a loss. It is a chance to find a better way.
The stone sings because it has something to say. We do not need to understand the words. We just need to listen.
The cord is not the problem. The problem is the way you tie it.
Giving does not mean losing. It means starting a circle.
A shelter is not just walls and roof. It is willingness. And willingness can hold anyone.
The knot that holds the storm is the knot that is tied with care, not with fear.
A cord that breaks is not a failure. It is a chance to tie it again, together.
The path that remembers the blind is a path that remembers everyone.
Memory is not in things. It is in the act of remembering.
You do not need to fix grief. You just need to hold it, and let it be held.
Hakaka sat on the bank, her hands empty. No cord. No loop. No knot. She was doing nothing. And it was enough.

What remains is not a thing. It is a way. The way of the weir: leave a gap. The way of the oven: wait until the wait turns sweet. The way of the ledger: write what happened, not what should have. The way of the watch: if you hear it, move. The way of the unknot: the open hand, waiting, without forcing.
These are not rules. They are the shape of survival, pressed into story.
And somewhere, on an ordinary day, a woman sits with her hands empty, listening. That is enough.
